To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) we have developed an approach for developer identification in multi-repository studies that allows the anonymization of information while keeping a track of identities; and 2) we have shown that our approach can be successfully applied to a case study, the GNOME project.
we propose a methodology for developer identification in integrated data from various data sources, and a data format for the anonymized distribution and the tracking of developer identities.

the methodology we propose allows to: - identify developers across multiple data sources; - anonymize the data; - allow partial merging with new sources; - provide a data structure to allow the tracking of identities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the different identities of developers in software projects, and the tracking, anonymization and integration of data from different sources.
the problem of how to integrate data from different repositories, and how to deal with the different identities that a single developer may use in different contexts.

the problem of identifying the many identities of a developer when mining data from different repositories and sources, and with the development of a methodology that allows the anonymization of data, and the tracking and identification of developers for verification purposes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our approach is useful for integrating data sources and for tracking developers across repositories.
the approach presented in this paper is useful for the identification of developers in multi-repository data, and it can be easily extended to new data sources.
this paper presents a novel approach for the integration of information from different data sources, and the identification of developers across different repositories.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, by using the proposed approach, the data from different repositories can be integrated in order to obtain a more complete view of the software development process, without the need for developers to use the same identity for interacting with all the different tools.

we present a methodology for the integration of data from various software repositories, and the identification of developers in the resulting integrated data, which can be used for performing multi-repository studies.
, by applying this approach to the GNOME project, we were able to track the activities of 1,000 developers, who were previously identified as 1,800.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the identification of developers is a complex issue in the context of software repositories.
, by applying the proposed approach, the integration of different data sources is possible and, therefore, the study of developers in different contexts is possible.

it is possible to perform studies with integrated data from various repositories without the need to have all the data in the same repository, which would be a very difficult task in many cases, and that it is possible, and even desirable to keep the information anonymous, and to allow the tracking of identities when needed.
